title: Foraging sloes from blackthorn in autumn
subtitle: Harvest window, the frost rule, and gin preparation
excerpt: Sloe is the small, astringent fruit of blackthorn, ripening in UK hedgerows from September through November. Too astringent to eat raw, sloes are frozen or pricked and steeped in spirit to make sloe gin or vodka. The first frosts soften the skins naturally.
sourceNotes: Richard Mabey, Food for Free (1972); John Wright, The Forager's Calendar (2019); BSBI species accounts for Prunus spinosa; Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

glossaryTerms.definition: Matching three independent visual, scent, or habitat features before eating any wild plant. All three must match; a single mismatch means stop.
A wild plant that resembles an edible species closely enough to cause misidentification. Many look-alikes are toxic.

content.text: Sloe (Prunus spinosa) is the small, blue-black fruit of blackthorn, ripening along UK hedgerows from September through November. Sloes are far too astringent to eat raw; they are frozen or pricked and steeped in gin or vodka with sugar to make sloe gin. Freezing mimics the softening effect of the first frosts and makes the skins easier to pierce; even one night at -18°C works. Verify your identification before eating; if in doubt, do not eat.
Apply the
rule-of-three identification
: confirm (1) the small, round, dark blue-black fruit with a dusty blue bloom, (2) the dense, thorny blackthorn shrub, and (3) the hedgerow or scrubland habitat. All three must match.
ID features
Fruit: round, 8 to 15 mm across, dark blue-black with a dusty blue-grey bloom. A central stone inside. Single fruit, not a cluster.
Shrub: dense, very thorny, with rigid thorns up to 30 mm long. Flowers white in March and April before the leaves appear, a key feature of blackthorn.
Leaves: small, oval, finely toothed, 2 to 4 cm long. Appear after the flowers.
Poisonous look-alikes
Sloe has one main UK
look-alike plant
worth checking in hedgerows.

Deadly nightshade (Atropa belladonna): shiny round black berries, but the plant is non-thorny and herbaceous with large oval leaves and bell-shaped flowers. Grows in similar hedgerow and scrubland habitats. Extremely toxic.

Bittersweet nightshade (Solanum dulcamara): red or black berries in small clusters, on a scrambling plant with purple star-shaped flowers. Not as acutely toxic as deadly nightshade but causes digestive distress. No thorns, no bloom.
When and how to harvest

Pick from mid-September through November. The traditional advice is to wait until after the first frost; if there has been none by October, freeze the sloes for 24 hours before steeping. Harvest with gloves: the thorns of blackthorn are long and sharp. Use secateurs to clip the fruiting twigs into a bag, then strip the berries at home.
Leave roughly a third of the berries on each plant for birds.
After harvesting

Rinse in cold water and pat dry. Freeze on a tray in a single layer for at least 24 hours. Once frozen, pack into a sterilised jar, add sugar, and pour over gin or vodka to cover. Seal and leave for at least three months, shaking once a week. The gin is ready by Christmas if started in late September.
Legal and ethical

The Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and Theft Act 1968 allow collection of fruit from hedgerows and common land for personal use. Private land requires the landowner's permission. Sloe is abundant in UK hedgerows; there is no conservation concern with personal picking.

rows.symptom: Sloe gin is still very bitter after three months
rows.cause: Insufficient sugar, or skins not pierced or frozen before steeping
rows.fix: Add more sugar to the jar and leave for a further month. Freezing before steeping is important; skins that were not frozen or pricked may not have released the flavour fully.

rows.symptom: Cannot tell whether fruit is sloe or deadly nightshade
rows.cause: Confusion between two dark hedgerow fruits
rows.fix: Sloe grows on a dense, very thorny shrub with a dusty blue bloom on the fruit; nightshade is non-thorny and herbaceous with shiny berries. If in any doubt, do not harvest.
